solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Murder duet with this big woman in United States

indicators.note: to murder a piece of music is to mangle it, so the letters of the duet and this word together are jumbled

parts.note: the twelve letters that the jumble must produce
the letters added to the unknown word before the jumble

explanation.surface: A grim tale of a large woman in America killing a singing partnership.
explanation.walkthrough: A composite anagram: 'Murder' says DUET plus 'this' (the answer) rearranged gives UNITED STATES, so take DUET's letters away from UNITED STATES and rearrange what remains.
explanation.definitionFit: A female member of the giant Titans of Greek myth, hence any huge woman.

clue.text: Excessively blast over roundabout?

parts.note: a blast on a horn or whistle is a toot
O is the cricket abbreviation for an over
a roundabout is circular, like the letter O

explanation.surface: Someone complains that sounding a horn at a traffic roundabout is overdoing it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'roundabout' is the road junction in the surface but only a ring shape here, the letter O.
explanation.definitionFit: The doubled form is a dated colloquial intensifier meaning far too much, overly so.

clue.text: Abstinent native of S America

definitions.meaning: abstinent is TT, teetotal, and the two letters spelt out as they are said
a small South American monkey, the titi, also spelt this way

explanation.surface: A teetotal inhabitant of South America.
explanation.walkthrough: The first sense works by spelling out the letters TT (teetotal) as words; the second is a little South American monkey.
explanation.definitionFit: Spelt-out letters for teetotal, plus an alternative name of the titi monkey of South American forests.

clue.text: A Verne trilogy would seal this deal

indicators.note: to seal something is to enclose it, so the long string of names holds the wanted letters and its spare ends are shed

parts.note: the surname of Jules Verne written out three times in a row
the opening three letters of the triple string, outside the seal
the closing two letters of the triple string, outside the seal

explanation.surface: A publisher might clinch a contract with a set of three Jules Verne novels.
explanation.walkthrough: Write the novelist's surname three times running; 'would seal this' says the answer sits sealed inside that string, minus its first three and last two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: British slang for hire purchase, a credit arrangement paid off in instalments over time.

clue.text: Experiences highs and lows: going North, South used to be East and vice versa

parts.note: the compass points the other way round: south then east, abbreviated

indicators.note: in a down clue going north means reading upwards, so the run of letters is reversed

parts.note: used to be means was

explanation.surface: A puzzling direction about compass points swapping places, like a confused traveller.
explanation.walkthrough: 'going North' turns S WAS E upwards into E SAW S; 'vice versa' supplies the points the other way, S and E, at the front.
explanation.definitionFit: To go up and down alternately, like a plank on a pivot, is to have ups and downs.

clue.text: Two who backed Knight for so long!

indicators.note: two of them means the backing singer's name is written twice

parts.note: Gladys Knight's backing group was the Pips, so one of them is a Pip

explanation.surface: A farewell from a pair of backing singers to the star they supported.
explanation.walkthrough: Gladys Knight and the Pips were a US soul group; 'Knight' looks like a chess piece or a title.
explanation.definitionFit: An old-fashioned British upper-class way of saying goodbye, like cheerio.

clue.text: Curry, say, with steaming rice containing fish…

indicators.note: the rearranged grain holds the fish within it
steaming rice is being cooked and stirred, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: a skate is a flat fish

explanation.surface: An Indian meal: a curry served with steamed rice and some fish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Curry' is not food: John Curry was a British Olympic figure-skating champion. ICER (from 'steaming' rice) takes SKATE inside.
explanation.definitionFit: John Curry won Olympic gold in 1976 as a figure skater, an example of someone performing on ice.

clue.text: …lots of piping chips served up? Brother's tucking in

indicators.note: the sibling is tucked inside the rearranged letters
chips served up are dished out in a new arrangement, so the letters are shuffled

parts.note: bro is a short form of brother

explanation.surface: Plenty of chips dished up while a brother tucks in hungrily.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tucking in' looks like eating; here it puts the sibling inside the jumble that 'served up' makes, PICHS.
explanation.definitionFit: Pieces of classical Highland bagpipe music, so plural tunes played on the pipes.

clue.text: Exotic bird collector in garden spreading fresh peat

indicators.note: the shuffled letters spread round the tool, enclosing it
fresh suggests a new arrangement of the letters of the peat

parts.note: a rake gathers up leaves in the garden

explanation.surface: A gardener spreading new peat finds an exotic bird on the lawn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fresh' scrambles the soil's letters into PA and ET, which then spread around the garden tool.
explanation.definitionFit: A small long-tailed tropical parrot, a colourful bird from distant lands.

clue.text: Survey one in group of Urban Hymns that was painful to cover

indicators.note: the cry of pain wraps around the rest, covering it

parts.note: ow is what you say when something hurts

indicators.note: the numeral goes inside the band's name

parts.note: Urban Hymns is a 1997 album by the British band The Verve
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A critic's look back at a hit album, with one track that hurt to cover.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cover' suggests a band recording another's song; here the cry of pain wraps round the band name with the numeral inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A survey is a general, broad look at a subject, a summary from above.

clue.text: N African pair of half-hearted porters?

indicators.note: a pair means the trimmed drink is written twice
the drink's heart is a double vowel, and half of it is dropped

parts.note: porter is a dark beer

explanation.surface: A question about a North African duo of unenthusiastic luggage carriers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'porters' are not bag carriers but a dark beer; BEER loses one of its two middle letters ('half-hearted') to give BER, written twice.
explanation.definitionFit: A member of the indigenous Amazigh peoples of North Africa, from Morocco to Libya.

clue.text: I don't agree there's much rush, but every second counts

indicators.note: only the second, fourth, sixth and eighth letters are counted and kept

explanation.surface: Someone disputes that there is any need to hurry, though time matters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'every second counts' sounds like urgency, but it picks the even letters of MUCH RUSH.
explanation.definitionFit: A casual spoken noise of refusal or disagreement, the opposite of a nod.

clue.text: Nothing against being human, do this every beat with wit

parts.note: O is zero, nothing
V is short for versus, against
to err is human, says Pope, so a human does this
every one means each

explanation.surface: Odd advice to face down nothingness, as a human, by sparring wittily at every beat.
explanation.walkthrough: Alexander Pope wrote 'To err is human', so 'being human, do this' is ERR. 'beat' in the surface is a rhythm, but in the definition it means defeat.
explanation.definitionFit: In an older sense, to get the better of someone by cunning, outwitting them.

clue.text: One's opening criticisms

definitions.meaning: a joke of the door-rapping kind, who's there, starts with these two words
adverse comments or pans, said twice

explanation.walkthrough: 'One' is a kind of joke, the type that begins with a double rap at the door; the second sense is two hostile remarks.
explanation.definitionFit: The opening line of a children's door-rapping joke, and also two pieces of criticism.

clue.text: Mythical reason for fertility of Ellis Island

indicators.note: the goddess is made of letters from the two words, lying inside them

explanation.surface: Why the immigration station at Ellis Island was so fruitful, a myth.
explanation.walkthrough: Ellis Island is the New York immigration station; the answer sits across its two words.
explanation.definitionFit: The Egyptian goddess worshipped as a mother deity and bringer of fruitfulness.

clue.text: Joint women wanted to enter were it not for the sensational reaction

indicators.note: the joint and the women go inside the word for except

parts.note: save means except, as in all save one
the hock is the joint in an animal's hind leg

explanation.surface: A shady bar would have caused a scandal, but for women wanting in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Joint' looks like a dive or nightclub, but it is the leg joint HOCK; 'wanted' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A wave of strong public feeling spreading after a startling event, like a blast front.

clue.text: Very attractive, that woman putting ring in camera socket

parts.note: hot means sexy, very attractive

indicators.note: the ring goes inside the pronoun for that woman

parts.note: she refers to that woman
O is ring-shaped

explanation.surface: A glamorous woman puts a ring into a socket on her camera.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ring' looks like jewellery, but it is just the round letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The metal bracket on top of a camera where a flashgun slides and connects.

clue.text: Implement hacked off head basically just to get a thrill

parts.note: a fork is an eating or garden implement

indicators.note: the head letter goes to the base, which in a down clue is the bottom

parts.note: hacked off means fed up, sick of it

explanation.surface: Someone takes a knife or fork and cuts off a head just for fun.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hacked off' sounds violent but means annoyed, SICK; 'head basically' sends its head S to the base, giving ICKS.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something for kicks is doing it only for the excitement or fun of it.

clue.text: Tells, or tells again? There's a change to construe

indicators.note: a change to the word means its letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A puzzle over whether someone narrates or repeats, with a reinterpretation to make.
explanation.walkthrough: Three routes: 'Tells' (narrates), 'tells again' (counts again, as tellers count votes) and 'a change to' rearranging CONSTRUE.
explanation.definitionFit: To narrate a story, and to count again as an election teller does.

clue.text: Develop sufficiently (about 67 per cent) to choose dresses

indicators.note: to dress something is to clothe it, so the word for choosing wraps round the rest

parts.note: to opt is to choose

indicators.note: roughly two thirds of the six letters, four, are kept and the last two dropped

parts.note: enough means sufficiently

explanation.surface: A shopper picks dresses that are almost sufficiently developed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about 67 per cent' keeps four of the six letters (two thirds), and 'dresses' wraps the word for choosing around them.
explanation.definitionFit: To unfold or expand, as a bud or a story grows and widens out.

clue.text: See you knot lace article

parts.note: to tat is to make knotted lace by hand
a is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A shopkeeper's farewell after selling a lace item.
explanation.walkthrough: 'See you' looks like part of the surface's speech but is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A casual British farewell, much like goodbye or bye-bye.

clue.text: Bellow when one's not allowed on board old ferry

indicators.note: the letter for one is not allowed to stay on, so it is removed

parts.note: to bellow is to roar
A means one, as in a dog

explanation.surface: Someone shouts angrily when refused passage on an old ferry.
explanation.walkthrough: ROAR loses A and gains O.
explanation.definitionFit: Short for roll-on roll-off, a vessel that vehicles drive on and off.

clue.text: Releasing BO, robe stank — awfully gross? None more so

indicators.note: letting go of the body odour letters means they are taken out of the pool
the remaining letters are put together in an awful, jumbled order

parts.note: BO is body odour

explanation.surface: A robe gives off body odour and stinks horribly, the grossest of all.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove B and O from ROBE STANK and rearrange the other letters ('awfully').
explanation.definitionFit: The superlative of rank in its sense of foul, coarse or flagrant, so the most gross.

clue.text: Audible followers of so-so children's character?

indicators.note: audible says the notes are heard spoken, then spelt as the name

parts.note: in tonic sol-fa la follows so, so after two so notes come two la notes

explanation.surface: Fans of an ordinary children's TV figure can be heard cheering.
explanation.walkthrough: In sol-fa (do, re, mi, fa, so, la, ti) la follows so. Laa-Laa is the yellow Teletubby.
explanation.definitionFit: Laa-Laa is a yellow Teletubby from the BBC television show for toddlers.

clue.text: Kcit sets enigmas, fixing unpleasant sucker

indicators.note: the words hold the answer fixed within them, held in place across three words

explanation.surface: A setter called Kcit compiles puzzles while dealing with a nasty bloodsucker.
explanation.walkthrough: Kcit is a real crossword setter (Tick backwards), and a tick is itself a bloodsucker, a decoy.
explanation.definitionFit: An African fly that feeds on blood and spreads sleeping sickness.

clue.text: See 13
Was reason for trapeze artist's injury rejected by section cutters?

indicators.note: by means beside, so the letter sits next to the rest
rejected means thrown back, so this phrase is read from end to start

parts.note: taken as written
a trapeze artist falls and is hurt because there was no safety net

explanation.surface: A puzzling question about a trapeze injury and whether section heads were to blame.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Was reason for trapeze artist's injury' is WAS NO NET; 'rejected' turns it back to TENON SAW.
explanation.definitionFit: Fine-toothed backed saws used for cutting joints in carpentry, a type of cutting tool.

clue.text: See 3
May couples dance?

indicators.note: couples are pairs, so the word is written twice

parts.note: may means can, has permission

explanation.surface: A question of whether pairs of partners are allowed on the dance floor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'May' looks like the month; 'couples' doubles CAN.
explanation.definitionFit: A lively high-kicking French music-hall dance from the Moulin Rouge era.

clue.text: Clever at manipulating sausage

indicators.note: manipulating means handling and shaping, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone skilled at handling a sausage.
explanation.definitionFit: A smoked pork sausage, made in Germany and France.

clue.text: Old taxes being trimmed by Hitler's bodyguard

indicators.note: the two letters border the other word, framing it as a trim does

parts.note: the SS began as Hitler's personal protection squad
esse is Latin for being, existence

explanation.surface: Historic levies cut back by the Nazi elite guard.
explanation.walkthrough: ESSE (Latin, being) sits between the two S letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A variant spelling of cesses, old local rates or levies, especially in Scotland and Ireland.

clue.text: Daydream brings reversal of new line in look

indicators.note: the reversed line sits inside the word for looking

parts.note: to stare is to look fixedly

indicators.note: reversal says the word for a new line is turned backwards

parts.note: a zag is a fresh line in a new direction after a zig

explanation.surface: A dreamer's mind wanders when a change of direction appears in their view.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reversal of' turns the zigzag's second stroke backwards, GAZ, and 'in' places it inside the look before its final letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To gaze at the heavens, figuratively to be absorbed in impractical dreaming.
